children.value: Five time-lag options are compared in this study (see
processing versions

for the exact settings). Four of
them start from one exploratory run,
CM-W

, and use its peak lag distribution
to configure themselves; the fifth,
PWB OPT

, is an independent method. The
flowchart shows how they relate, and the notes below say when each is
appropriate.
The five variants compared in this study.

CM-W (variant 1) is one wide
covariance-maximisation run (Nemitz steps 1 to 3): it keeps its own lags and
yields the distribution peak (nominal lag) and the distribution range. The peak
is the default fallback for variants 2 and 3 and the fixed lag for variant 4; the
range sets the narrow window for variant 3. PWB OPT (variant 5) is independent.
The Nemitz et al. (2018) fallback hierarchy is shown separately as a reference
path:
When to use what
1. CM-W (wide window, no default).

The exploratory first pass. It searches
the whole 0 to 10 s window every half-hour with no fallback, so its output
reveals the lag distribution and its modal peak, which options 2 to 4 build on.
With nothing constraining the search, it is the most exposed to the
covariance-maximisation (“mirroring”) bias for low signal-to-noise gases like
N₂O: per half-hour the lag that maximises the absolute covariance is picked,
inflating the flux away from zero. Covariance can be maximised against the scalar
S of interest itself, or against an inert gas on the same analyzer (shared
sampling line, so the lag is easier to detect), whose lag is then applied to S.
Use it to characterise the lag and configure 2 to 4; treat its flux as the upper
bound of that bias, not the final answer.
2. CM-W + default.

The same wide window, but it falls back to the nominal lag
(the CM-W peak) whenever the search is unreliable. Use it for automatic
per-half-hour lags with a safety net against obviously wrong picks. It still
carries most of the mirroring bias, since the search range is unchanged.
3. CM-W CTR + default.

The search is constrained to a narrow window around
the peak, with the same fallback. The narrow window curbs the mirroring bias
while still letting the lag track real variation within a known range. Use it
when the true lag is well constrained and reasonably stable. This is the
recommended covariance-maximisation option.
4. Constant lag.

A single fixed lag at the CM-W peak, applied to every
half-hour. Use it when the lag is physically stable (for example a steady
closed-path setup) and you want to remove the covariance-maximisation bias
entirely. Most conservative budget, but ignores any real lag variation over time.
5. PWB OPT.

Independent of covariance maximisation and robust to the
mirroring bias. It is the reference method (Vitale et al. 2024): the benchmark
the covariance-maximisation options are judged against, and the default when a
bias-resistant lag is wanted without tuning a window by hand.
Rule of thumb
Run
CM-W

first: its peak distribution sets up 2 to 4, and its flux shows
how large the covariance-maximisation bias is for your gas.
For a covariance-maximisation flux, prefer the constrained
CM-W CTR

over
the wide-window variants: the narrow window is what limits the bias.
Use the
constant lag
only where the lag is genuinely stable.
Reach for
PWB OPT

when you want a bias-resistant lag with no window to
tune, or as the reference the other options are compared against.
